techs.bronzeWorking: Smiths who learned to alloy copper with tin produced tools and blades far harder than stone, and the age of bronze began. In the game it is the first real step toward a sturdy defence, putting the [Spearman](pedia:units/spearman) on the field, and it allows coastal cities to raise the [Colossus](pedia:buildings/colossus).
techs.masonry: Cutting and stacking stone let early peoples build walls, granaries and monuments meant to outlast their builders. Masonry gives your cities [City Walls](pedia:buildings/walls) and the seat of government, and it starts the race for the Pyramids. Workers also learn to raise outposts that watch over distant ground.
techs.alphabet: Reducing speech to a small set of symbols made recording ideas cheap enough for ordinary scribes and merchants. The Alphabet unlocks little on its own, but nearly every branch of learning grows from it, beginning with [Writing](pedia:techs/writing) and the mathematics that lead to engineering and trade.
techs.pottery: Fired clay vessels let farming communities store grain, oil and water through lean seasons. In the game Pottery provides the [Granary](pedia:buildings/granary), which helps a city keep part of its food after it grows, and it is one of the roots of seafaring through Map Making.
techs.theWheel: The wheel transformed transport and warfare once animals could pull carts and fighting platforms. Discovering it reveals [Horses](pedia:resources/horses) on the map and lets you build the [Chariot](pedia:units/chariot), the first fast attacker, provided your cities are connected to a source of horses.
techs.warriorCode: Every early society developed customs that turned hunters into disciplined fighters, archers chief among them. Warrior Code gives you the [Archer](pedia:units/archer), a cheap unit that can attack as well as defend, and it leads on to Horseback Riding and, with Polytheism, to Monarchy.
techs.ceremonialBurial: Rituals for honouring the dead are among the oldest signs of religious belief. This advance lets cities build the [Temple](pedia:buildings/temple), the first tool for keeping a growing population content, and it opens the path toward Mysticism and Polytheism.
techs.ironWorking: Iron ore was more common than tin and copper, and once furnaces grew hot enough it equipped whole armies. Iron Working reveals [Iron](pedia:resources/iron) deposits and, with access to one, the [Swordsman](pedia:units/swordsman). It is also needed for Construction and the walls, roads and arenas that follow.
techs.writing: Writing let rulers keep records, issue laws and send messages across distance without relying on memory. In the game it allows diplomats to establish embassies and makes military alliances possible, and it is the gateway to Literature, Philosophy, Code of Laws and Map Making.
techs.mysticism: Mysticism sought hidden meaning in the stars, omens and the will of the gods, and priests grew powerful as interpreters. It allows the [Oracle](pedia:buildings/oracle), an early wonder of faith that helps keep citizens calm, and it leads on to Polytheism and later to Astronomy.
techs.mathematics: Counting, geometry and measurement made it possible to plan buildings, divide land and aim siege engines. Mathematics provides the [Catapult](pedia:units/catapult), your first unit able to bombard cities from a distance, and it is the basis of Currency and Construction.
techs.philosophy: Thinkers in many lands began asking how one ought to live and how the world is ordered, laying foundations for science and politics. Philosophy allows the [Mausoleum of Mausollos](pedia:buildings/mausoleumOfMausollos) and, together with Code of Laws, leads to [The Republic](pedia:techs/theRepublic).
techs.codeOfLaws: A written code replaced the whims of rulers with known rules and penalties applied to all. Code of Laws gives the [Courthouse](pedia:buildings/courthouse), which reduces corruption in distant cities, and together with Philosophy it opens the way to [The Republic](pedia:techs/theRepublic).
techs.literature: Epics, histories and poetry preserved the memory and values of whole peoples. Literature lets cities build the [Library](pedia:buildings/library), raising science and culture, and it allows the [Great Library](pedia:buildings/greatLibrary). It is optional for reaching the Middle Ages, so you can postpone it.
techs.mapMaking: Charting coastlines and currents let sailors venture beyond sight of home and return. Map Making brings the [Galley](pedia:units/galley) for carrying settlers and troops along the coast, the [Harbor](pedia:buildings/harbor) and the Great Lighthouse, and it allows rights of passage agreements with other civilizations.
techs.horsebackRiding: Mounting horses directly gave riders speed that no foot soldier could match. Horseback Riding brings the [Horseman](pedia:units/horseman), a fast raider and explorer that needs access to [Horses](pedia:resources/horses). Mounted units can withdraw from losing fights against slower foes.
techs.polytheism: Belief in many gods, each ruling a part of nature or society, was the faith of most early civilizations. Polytheism allows the [Temple of Artemis](pedia:buildings/templeOfArtemis), a great shrine of the ancient world, and together with Warrior Code it leads to [Monarchy](pedia:techs/monarchy).
techs.currency: Coins of fixed weight and value made trade far easier than barter. Currency introduces the [Marketplace](pedia:buildings/marketplace), which increases both luxuries and tax income in a city, and it leads to Banking and the commercial branch of the tree.
techs.theRepublic: Citizens of early republics chose their leaders and shared in decisions, which encouraged commerce and civic pride. This advance unlocks the [Republic](pedia:governments/republic), a government that boosts trade at the cost of tolerance for long wars. It is optional for reaching the Middle Ages.
techs.monarchy: A hereditary ruler backed by the nobility and priesthood gave early states stable leadership. This advance unlocks [Monarchy](pedia:governments/monarchy), a sturdy government for a militaristic empire, and the [Hanging Gardens](pedia:buildings/hangingGardens). It is optional for reaching the Middle Ages.
techs.construction: Arches, concrete and organised labour produced amphitheatres, aqueducts and long defensive walls. Construction gives the [Aqueduct](pedia:buildings/aqueduct), so cities can grow beyond their early size, and the [Colosseum](pedia:buildings/colosseum). It also allows the Great Wall and lets workers build fortresses and barricades for holding passes and borders.
techs.monotheism: Faith in a single god inspired great cathedrals and drew whole nations together. As one of the first advances of the Middle Ages, it lets cities build the [Cathedral](pedia:buildings/cathedral), the most powerful early answer to unhappiness in large cities, and it leads to Theology and Chivalry.
techs.feudalism: Lords granted land to vassals in return for military service, binding society into a chain of loyalties. Feudalism unlocks the [Feudalism](pedia:governments/feudalism) government and the [Pikeman](pedia:units/pikeman), a strong defender against mounted attack. It also allows Sun Tzu's Art of War.
techs.engineering: Medieval engineers built bridges, mills, cranes and siege machines on a scale the ancient world had rarely attempted. Engineering lets roads bridge rivers, gives the [Trebuchet](pedia:units/trebuchet) for battering fortified cities from a distance, and allows workers to [plant forests](pedia:workerJobs/plantForest) on open land.
techs.theology: Theologians attempted to reconcile faith with reason and to give religion a systematic body of teaching taught in schools. Theology allows the [Sistine Chapel](pedia:buildings/sistineChapel), a great wonder of faith, and it leads to Education and to the [Printing Press](pedia:techs/printingPress).
techs.chivalry: Knighthood combined heavy cavalry with a code of honour that shaped medieval warfare. Chivalry brings the [Knight](pedia:units/knight), a strong mounted attacker that needs both horses and iron, and the [Knights Templar](pedia:buildings/knightsTemplar). It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.invention: Clever mechanisms, from mechanical clocks to new weapons of war, appeared across the medieval world. Invention unlocks [Leonardo's Workshop](pedia:buildings/leonardosWorkshop), which makes upgrading outdated units much cheaper, and the [Longbowman](pedia:units/longbowman), a strong archer. It leads directly to Gunpowder.
techs.printingPress: Movable type made books cheap and spread new ideas faster than any authority could control them. The Printing Press lets you trade advances with other civilizations through diplomacy and is a prerequisite of [Democracy](pedia:techs/democracy). It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.musicTheory: Composers developed harmony, notation and new forms that made music an art of great complexity. Music Theory allows [J.S. Bach's Cathedral](pedia:buildings/jsBachsCathedral), which calms citizens across the whole continent. It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.education: Universities brought scholars together to study law, medicine and natural philosophy, and to pass that knowledge on. Education gives the [University](pedia:buildings/university), a major boost to research in a city, and it leads to Banking, Astronomy and Music Theory, so few civilizations can skip it.
techs.gunpowder: An explosive mixture of saltpeter, sulphur and charcoal ended the long dominance of castles and armoured knights. Gunpowder reveals [Saltpeter](pedia:resources/saltpeter) on the map and gives the [Musketman](pedia:units/musketman), a defender strong enough to hold cities against most attackers for centuries.
techs.banking: Banks held deposits, issued credit and financed trade ventures and wars. Banking lets cities build the [Bank](pedia:buildings/bank), which raises both tax income and luxuries, and it leads to Economics and, with the Printing Press, to Democracy.
techs.astronomy: Careful observation of the heavens revealed that the Earth is not the centre of the universe. Astronomy allows [Copernicus' Observatory](pedia:buildings/copernicusObservatory), brings the [Caravel](pedia:units/caravel) and the Explorer for charting new lands, and opens trade routes across the open sea.
techs.chemistry: Alchemy gave way to systematic study of substances and how they combine. Chemistry unlocks no unit or building of its own, but it is a key link in the tree, leading to Physics and to Metallurgy with its cannon and coastal fortresses.
techs.democracy: Representative government gave citizens a voice in the state and protection under the law. This advance unlocks [Democracy](pedia:governments/democracy), the government with the strongest commerce and lowest corruption, though its people quickly tire of war. It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.economics: Economists studied markets, prices and the division of labour as systems that could be understood. Economics allows [Smith's Trading Company](pedia:buildings/smithsTradingCompany) and makes converting production into gold more effective. It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.navigation: Better instruments and charts let ships cross oceans and reliably find their way back. Navigation allows [Magellan's Voyage](pedia:buildings/magellansVoyage), extends trade routes across deep water and lets you exchange world maps with other civilizations. It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.physics: Natural philosophers measured motion, force and light with a new mathematical precision. Physics opens no unit or building by itself, but it is a crossroads of the tree, leading both to [Magnetism](pedia:techs/magnetism) and its ocean-going warships and to the Theory of Gravity.
techs.metallurgy: Better furnaces and casting methods produced reliable cannon of bronze and iron in large numbers. Metallurgy brings the [Cannon](pedia:units/cannon), a powerful siege weapon that needs iron and saltpeter, and the [Coastal Fortress](pedia:buildings/coastalFortress) for protecting harbour cities from enemy ships.
techs.freeArtistry: Patrons and free markets let artists work for the public rather than only for church and crown. Free Artistry allows [Shakespeare's Theater](pedia:buildings/shakespearesTheater), which keeps one city's people content even as it grows very large. It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.theoryOfGravity: A single law of gravitation explained both falling apples and the orbits of planets. The Theory of Gravity allows [Newton's University](pedia:buildings/newtonsUniversity), a great boost to research in one city, and is a natural target for a science-focused civilization.
techs.magnetism: The magnetic compass let sailors hold a course far from land and in any weather. Magnetism brings the [Frigate](pedia:units/frigate) and the [Galleon](pedia:units/galleon), allowing real naval warfare and large overseas expeditions, and it opens trade across the oceans.
techs.militaryTradition: Professional officer corps, constant drill and staff schools turned warfare into a discipline of its own. Military Tradition brings [Cavalry](pedia:units/cavalry), the fastest attacker before engines, and the [Military Academy](pedia:buildings/militaryAcademy). It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.nationalism: The idea that a people shares one nation and one destiny mobilised whole populations. Nationalism gives the [Rifleman](pedia:units/rifleman), allows drafting citizens and putting the economy on a war footing, and makes mutual protection pacts and trade embargoes possible.
techs.steamPower: The steam engine supplied power on a scale that muscles and water wheels never could. Steam Power reveals [Coal](pedia:resources/coal) and lets workers lay [railroads](pedia:workerJobs/railroad), which make movement along them free and increase the output of tiles. It also leads to Ironclads and Industrialization.
techs.medicine: Physicians began to study disease systematically and treat it with real success. Medicine has no unit or building of its own, but it is the path to [Sanitation](pedia:techs/sanitation) and, with Electricity, to the Scientific Method.
techs.communism: Communism promised a society without classes, run by the state on behalf of the workers. It unlocks the [Communism](pedia:governments/communism) government, which spreads corruption evenly across a large empire, and the [Police Station](pedia:buildings/policeStation). It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.industrialization: Factories and mass labour turned out goods in quantities no workshop could match, and towns grew into cities. Industrialization gives the [Factory](pedia:buildings/factory) and allows [Universal Suffrage](pedia:buildings/universalSuffrage). Factories bring production, but also the first serious pollution.
techs.electricity: Harnessing electric current opened the way to telegraphs, lighting and electric motors. In the game Electricity lets workers irrigate any suitable tile even without a nearby river or lake, which turns dry land into farmland. It leads to Replaceable Parts and the Scientific Method.
techs.scientificMethod: Hypothesis, experiment and open publication turned scattered discoveries into a self-correcting enterprise that sped up every field. The Scientific Method allows the [Theory of Evolution](pedia:buildings/theoryOfEvolution), a wonder that grants free advances, and leads on to Atomic Theory.
techs.sanitation: Sewers and clean water supplies cut the death toll from epidemics in crowded cities. Sanitation brings the [Hospital](pedia:buildings/hospital), which lets cities grow past their previous limit, and it ends the disease that afflicts cities working flood plains. It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.espionage: Industrial nations set up permanent agencies to gather the secrets of rivals and protect their own. Espionage allows the [Intelligence Agency](pedia:buildings/intelligenceAgency) for running spy missions against other civilizations, and the secret police headquarters. It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.theCorporation: Limited-liability companies pooled capital from many investors to build railways, mines and factories on a vast scale. The Corporation gives the [Stock Exchange](pedia:buildings/stockExchange), extending the gold and luxury income of a city with a bank, and it leads to Refining and Steel.
techs.refining: Distillation turned thick crude petroleum into fuels and lubricants for a new generation of machines. Refining reveals [Oil](pedia:resources/oil), the resource that will power ships, tanks and aircraft for the rest of the game. Securing oil fields early is often decisive in later wars.
techs.steel: Cheap mass-produced steel was stronger and more flexible than iron, and it reshaped bridges, buildings and battleships. Steel opens no unit by itself, but together with Refining it leads to [Combustion](pedia:techs/combustion) and the modern navy.
techs.atomicTheory: Experiments showed that matter is made of atoms with their own inner structure. Atomic Theory has no direct unit or building, but it leads to [Electronics](pedia:techs/electronics) and is an early step on the long road to atomic power.
techs.combustion: The internal combustion engine burned fuel inside its cylinders, making it far lighter and more efficient than steam. Combustion brings the [Destroyer](pedia:units/destroyer), cruiser and transport, all of which need [Oil](pedia:resources/oil), and leads to Flight and Mass Production.
techs.replaceableParts: Standardised, interchangeable parts made mass production and quick repairs possible, in factories and on the battlefield alike. This advance reveals [Rubber](pedia:resources/rubber), brings [Infantry](pedia:units/infantry) and Artillery, and doubles how quickly your workers complete every job, a huge boost for developing land.
techs.flight: Powered flight conquered the air within a few years of the first hops. Flight brings the [Fighter](pedia:units/fighter) and Bomber, lets cities build an [Airport](pedia:buildings/airport), and allows workers to build airfields for basing aircraft outside cities.
techs.amphibiousWar: Modern armies developed specialised troops, landing craft and tactics for storming defended shores. Amphibious War brings the [Marine](pedia:units/marine), which can attack a coastal city directly from a ship without landing first. It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.massProduction: Assembly lines turned out cars, ships and weapons by the thousand, and industrial nations could arm on an enormous scale. Mass Production brings the [Battleship](pedia:units/battleship), the Carrier and the Submarine, along with the [Commercial Dock](pedia:buildings/commercialDock), and leads to motorised armies.
techs.electronics: Vacuum tubes and circuits made radio and electrical engineering of every kind possible. Electronics allows the [Hydro Plant](pedia:buildings/hydroPlant) and the [Hoover Dam](pedia:buildings/hooverDam), clean power sources that boost factory output, and it leads to Advanced Flight.
techs.motorizedTransportation: Trucks and tracked vehicles freed armies from railheads, roads and horses. This advance brings the [Tank](pedia:units/tank), a powerful and fast attacker that needs both oil and rubber, and it is a key step toward [Advanced Flight](pedia:techs/advancedFlight) and the helicopter.
techs.advancedFlight: Larger, faster aircraft and the first practical helicopters extended air power over land and sea. Advanced Flight brings the [Helicopter](pedia:units/helicopter) and the Paratrooper and lets workers raise [radar towers](pedia:workerJobs/radarTower). It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.rocketry: Rocket engines carried payloads to heights and speeds no aircraft could reach. As an opening advance of the Modern era it reveals [Aluminum](pedia:resources/aluminum) and brings jet fighters, cruise missiles, and the mobile surface-to-air defences that protect armies from bombers.
techs.fission: Splitting the atom released enormous energy, for good and for terrible ends. Fission reveals [Uranium](pedia:resources/uranium) and allows both the [Manhattan Project](pedia:buildings/manhattanProject), which permits nuclear weapons for every civilization that can build them, and the United Nations.
techs.computers: Programmable machines took over calculation, communication and control in every part of society. Computers give the [Research Lab](pedia:buildings/researchLab) and the [SETI Program](pedia:buildings/setiProgram), both major boosts to science, and Mechanized Infantry, the toughest and most mobile defender of the modern age.
techs.recycling: Recovering materials from waste reduced both pollution and the demand for fresh raw materials. Recycling lets cities build the [Recycling Center](pedia:buildings/recyclingCenter), which sharply reduces the [pollution](pedia:concepts/pollution) caused by heavy industry, an important help for large industrial cities.
techs.spaceFlight: Rockets carried satellites and then people into orbit and beyond. Space Flight allows the [Apollo Program](pedia:buildings/apolloProgram) and the first spaceship parts, starting the race for a space victory, and it also brings the tactical nuclear missile, a smaller atomic weapon for the battlefield.
techs.nuclearPower: Controlled fission in reactors produced electricity in great quantity without burning coal or oil. Nuclear Power gives the [Nuclear Plant](pedia:buildings/nuclearPlant), a powerful boost to factory production that needs uranium and a nearby source of water, and that can melt down if its city falls into disorder.
techs.superconductor: Materials that carry electricity without resistance promised powerful magnets and nearly lossless power lines. Superconductor provides further spaceship components, the fuel cells and the life support system, and together with Satellites and Smart Weapons it leads to [Integrated Defense](pedia:techs/integratedDefense).
techs.miniaturization: Ever smaller components packed more computing power into less space, from pocket calculators to guidance systems. Miniaturization allows the [Offshore Platform](pedia:buildings/offshorePlatform), which lets water tiles yield shields, and the [Internet](pedia:buildings/internet) wonder, and it leads on to Genetics and Robotics.
techs.ecology: The study of how living things depend on each other made the costs of pollution plain to see. As an opening advance of the Modern era, Ecology gives the [Mass Transit System](pedia:buildings/massTransitSystem) and the [Solar Plant](pedia:buildings/solarPlant), both valuable tools for keeping a crowded industrial empire clean.
techs.syntheticFibers: Nylon, Kevlar and other man-made materials offered strength and lightness that natural fibres lacked. Synthetic Fibers brings [Modern Armor](pedia:units/modernArmor), the strongest land attacker in the game, and the Modern Paratrooper, along with parts of the spaceship's casing and storage.
techs.satellites: Orbiting satellites watch the world and relay communications around the globe. Satellites bring the [ICBM](pedia:units/icbm), the most feared weapon in the game, and the thrusters of the spaceship, and they lead on to Smart Weapons and Integrated Defense.
techs.theLaser: Coherent light found uses from surgery to communication and weapon targeting. The Laser leads to [Robotics](pedia:techs/robotics) and Smart Weapons and provides one of the parts needed to complete a spaceship, so a civilization racing for space cannot skip it.
techs.genetics: Decoding the genetic code opened the way to treating hereditary disease and reshaping living organisms. Genetics allows the [Cure for Cancer](pedia:buildings/cureForCancer), which makes citizens more content in every one of your cities, and Longevity, a further wonder of modern medicine.
techs.stealth: Aircraft shaped and coated to defeat radar could strike almost unseen, deep behind enemy lines. Stealth brings the [Stealth Fighter](pedia:units/stealthFighter) and the [Stealth Bomber](pedia:units/stealthBomber), the most advanced aircraft available, both needing oil and aluminum to build.
techs.smartWeapons: Guided munitions could find and hit a single target with remarkable accuracy, sparing everything around it. Smart Weapons enables precision bombing, which lets your aircraft aim at a chosen building in an enemy city, and it leads to [Integrated Defense](pedia:techs/integratedDefense).
techs.robotics: Robots took over dangerous and repetitive work in factories and on battlefields. Robotics gives the [Manufacturing Plant](pedia:buildings/manufacturingPlant), the greatest production building in the game, as well as Radar Artillery, the [AEGIS Cruiser](pedia:units/aegisCruiser) and the spaceship's stasis chamber.
techs.integratedDefense: Networks of sensors, computers and interceptors aimed to shield an entire nation from missile attack. Integrated Defense allows [Strategic Missile Defense](pedia:buildings/strategicMissileDefense), which gives your cities a chance to stop incoming nuclear missiles before they strike. It is the last advance of the tree.
techs.ironclads: Steam engines and iron armour made wooden warships obsolete almost overnight. This advance brings the [Ironclad](pedia:units/ironclad), a coastal warship that needs iron and coal and can dominate wooden fleets. It is optional for advancing to the next era.
techs.fascism: Fascism glorified the state and its leader and subordinated all of society to national power. It unlocks the [Fascism](pedia:governments/fascism) government, built for total war, which can rush production with forced labour. It is optional for advancing to the next era.

eras.ancient: The ancient era begins with a single band of settlers and ends with organised kingdoms. It is a race for land, for the first wonders and for the basic tools of government, faith and trade, and choices made here shape your whole empire.
eras.middle: In the Middle Ages religion, feudal loyalty and new learning define civilizations. Cathedrals and universities sustain larger cities, gunpowder ends the reign of knights, and ships begin to cross the oceans in search of new lands and trade.
eras.industrial: Steam, steel and factories transform production, and railroads tie empires together. New governments rise from mass politics, oil and rubber become vital, and wars are fought with rifles, ironclads, tanks and the first aircraft.
eras.modern: The modern era brings computers, nuclear power, jet aircraft and guided missiles. Pollution becomes a serious problem, nuclear weapons threaten every city, and the race to build a spaceship can decide the fate of the world.

terrains.desert: Dry, barren land that feeds almost no one on its own. Desert is mostly crossed rather than settled, though irrigation and an oasis make parts of it useful, and mines add a little production. Watch for saltpeter and oil beneath the sand, and incense in its trading towns.
terrains.plains: Open, gently rolling land that offers a balance of food and production. Plains suit both farms and roads and make good city sites. Irrigate them for growth or plant a forest for shields; horses, cattle, wheat, wines and ivory are common here.
terrains.grassland: Fertile meadows that make the best farmland of the early game. Grassland feeds cities well, especially when irrigated, and some tiles carry an outcrop that adds production. Cattle, wheat, horses, wines and tobacco are found here.
terrains.tundra: Cold, treeless land with a short growing season. Tundra supports only small populations and cannot be irrigated, but roads and mines help a little. Hunters find game and furs, and later ages discover oil and aluminum beneath the frozen soil.
terrains.floodPlain: River land renewed each year by silt-laden floods, among the richest farmland anywhere. Flood plains feed large cities, but they breed disease until [Sanitation](pedia:techs/sanitation) is known. They cannot be mined, so irrigation is the job that fits.
terrains.hills: Rolling high ground that is hard to cross but easy to defend. A city on hills is much safer, and mined hills are among the best production tiles in the game. Hills hold many valuable resources, including iron, coal, saltpeter and gold.
terrains.mountains: Steep peaks that slow every army and block wheeled units without a road. Mountains give the strongest defensive bonus and let units see farther, but no city can stand on them. Mines produce shields, and iron, gold, gems, coal and uranium are found here.
terrains.forest: Woodland that supplies timber and gives cover to defenders. Forests are a reliable source of shields early on and can be cleared for plains, which also sends a burst of production to the nearest city. Furs, game, silks, dyes and later rubber appear in them.
terrains.jungle: Dense tropical forest, hot, wet and hard to cross. Jungle is poor land for a city until it is cleared into grassland, a long job for workers. It hides valuable spices, silks, dyes, gems and tropical fruit, and later rubber and coal.
terrains.marsh: Waterlogged lowland that is slow to cross and difficult to settle or build on. Workers can drain marsh into grassland. Game and fish live here, and in later ages oil and rubber make some marshes worth holding.
terrains.volcano: An active cone of rock and ash, rich in mineral soil but unsafe to live on. Volcanoes cannot hold cities or most improvements, though they offer good production to a nearby city and a strong defensive position.
terrains.coast: Shallow water along the shore that provides food and trade to any city beside it. A [Harbor](pedia:buildings/harbor) makes coastal tiles much more productive. Early ships are safest here, and fish are the common resource.
terrains.sea: Deeper water beyond the coast, less productive but still workable by a city. Fish and whales are found here. Galleys and other early boats founder if they venture onto it, so open sea must wait for sturdier ships.
terrains.ocean: The open deep ocean, far from any shore, offers almost nothing to cities until an [Offshore Platform](pedia:buildings/offshorePlatform) is built. Only ships from the age of exploration onward can safely cross it.

resources.horses: Tamed herds that made riding and chariot warfare possible. Horses are a strategic resource revealed by The Wheel; you need access to them for chariots, horsemen, knights and cavalry. Horses never run out.
resources.iron: Iron ore, the foundation of better weapons and later of industry. This strategic resource is needed for swordsmen, pikemen, knights, cannon and early modern warships, and it is required to build the [Factory](pedia:buildings/factory). Iron deposits can be exhausted over time.
resources.saltpeter: A mineral salt that forms the chief ingredient of gunpowder. Revealed by [Gunpowder](pedia:techs/gunpowder), this strategic resource is needed for musketmen, cannon, cavalry and the frigates of the age of sail.
resources.coal: Fossil fuel that powered the industrial revolution. Revealed by [Steam Power](pedia:techs/steamPower), coal is needed for the Ironclad and the coal power plant, and the tile it occupies is highly productive.
resources.oil: Crude petroleum, the fuel of the modern world. Revealed by [Refining](pedia:techs/refining), oil is needed for most modern ships, all early aircraft and tanks, making it one of the most fought-over resources in the game.
resources.rubber: Natural latex from tropical trees, essential for tyres and seals. Revealed by [Replaceable Parts](pedia:techs/replaceableParts), rubber is needed for infantry, marines, tanks and mechanized infantry, and for the Mass Transit System.
resources.aluminum: A light, strong metal produced in large quantities only in modern times. Revealed by [Rocketry](pedia:techs/rocketry), aluminum is needed for jet aircraft, missiles, modern armor and most spaceship parts.
resources.uranium: A radioactive ore that fuels both power reactors and atomic weapons. Revealed by [Fission](pedia:techs/fission), uranium is needed for nuclear submarines, nuclear plants, nuclear missiles and the Manhattan Project.
resources.wines: Vineyards that produce wine for feasts and trade. Wines are a luxury: connecting them to your trade network makes citizens happier, and surplus can be traded to other civilizations for gold or goods.
resources.furs: Pelts from cold northern forests and tundra, prized for warmth and status. Furs are a luxury that makes connected cities happier and can be traded to rival civilizations.
resources.dyes: Rare colours extracted from plants and insects, once valued like precious metals. Dyes are a luxury that brings contentment to connected cities and is a useful bargaining good in diplomacy.
resources.incense: Fragrant resins burned in temples and palaces across the ancient world. Incense is a luxury that makes connected cities happier, and it is often found in desert and hill country.
resources.spices: Pepper, cinnamon and cloves, the cargo that launched voyages around the world. Spices are a luxury that keeps connected cities content and makes a good trade good.
resources.ivory: Tusks prized for carving and decoration. Ivory is a luxury that brings happiness to connected cities, and it is needed to build the [Statue of Zeus](pedia:buildings/statueOfZeus).
resources.silks: Fine cloth spun from silkworm cocoons, among the most valuable goods of ancient trade. Silks are a luxury that makes connected cities happier and adds commerce to the tile.
resources.gems: Precious stones mined from mountains and jungle. Gems are a luxury, the richest in commerce, and connecting them to your trade network keeps citizens happier.
resources.whales: Great sea mammals hunted for oil, meat and bone. Whales are a bonus resource that adds food, shields and commerce to a sea tile worked by a nearby city.
resources.game: Deer, elk and other wild animals in forest, tundra and marsh. Game is a bonus resource that adds food, making otherwise poor land able to support a city.
resources.fish: Rich fishing grounds along coasts and in shallow seas. Fish are a bonus resource that makes water tiles much better for feeding a growing city.
resources.cattle: Herds raised on open plains and grassland. Cattle are a bonus resource that adds both food and production, making them excellent early tiles.
resources.wheat: Wild or cultivated grain on fertile land. Wheat is a bonus resource that adds food, and an irrigated wheat tile can drive rapid city growth.
resources.gold: Veins of precious metal in hills and mountains. Gold is a bonus resource that adds a great deal of commerce to the tile, boosting your tax and science income.
resources.sugar: Sugar cane grown in warm climates. Sugar is a bonus resource that adds a little food and commerce to the tile.
resources.tropicalFruit: Bananas, mangoes and other fruit from the jungle. Tropical fruit is a bonus resource that adds food and commerce, helping a jungle city survive until the land is cleared.
resources.oasis: A spring in the desert surrounded by palms. An oasis is a bonus resource that adds food, turning a barren desert tile into a useful one.
resources.tobacco: A cash crop grown on grassland and hills. Tobacco is a bonus resource that adds commerce to the tile.

workerJobs.mine: Workers dig shafts and quarries to extract stone, ore and coal. A mine increases the shields of hills, mountains and other suitable terrain, and it replaces any irrigation on the tile. Mined hills are the backbone of a productive city.
workerJobs.irrigation: Workers dig channels that carry water to the fields. Irrigation increases food on suitable terrain, but needs fresh water from a river, a lake or another irrigated tile next to it until [Electricity](pedia:techs/electricity) is known. It replaces a mine.
workerJobs.fortress: Workers build earthworks and walls in open country. A fortress gives defending units a strong bonus, units inside exert a zone of control, and it is ideal for holding passes and borders. Requires [Construction](pedia:techs/construction).
workerJobs.road: Workers clear and pave a path across the land. Roads speed up movement greatly, connect cities so that resources and luxuries can be shared, and add commerce on most terrain. They are usually the first thing workers build. See [movement](pedia:concepts/movement).
workerJobs.railroad: Workers lay iron rails on an existing road. A railroad lets units move along it at no cost and increases the shields of tiles that already produce them. It needs [Steam Power](pedia:techs/steamPower) and access to iron.
workerJobs.plantForest: Workers plant trees on plains, grassland or tundra, turning the tile into forest. This gives up food in exchange for production and defensive cover. Requires [Engineering](pedia:techs/engineering).
workerJobs.clearForest: Workers cut down a forest, restoring the open land beneath it. The timber sends a one-time contribution of shields to the nearest city, a useful way to speed up early builds.
workerJobs.clearWetlands: Workers drain jungle or marsh and turn it into grassland. It is slow work, but it turns poor land into good farmland for a growing city.
workerJobs.clearDamage: Workers clean up pollution or a nuclear crater on a tile. Damaged tiles produce less and add to global warming, so it is important to clear them quickly. See [pollution](pedia:concepts/pollution).
workerJobs.airfield: Workers build a landing strip outside a city. An airfield lets aircraft be based and rebased away from cities, extending the reach of your air force. Requires [Flight](pedia:techs/flight).
workerJobs.radarTower: Workers erect a radar station. A radar tower gives your units nearby a better view of the area and helps defend against attack. Requires [Advanced Flight](pedia:techs/advancedFlight).
workerJobs.outpost: Workers build a watchtower. An outpost lets you see farther across the land, and even farther from hills or mountains, which makes it useful for watching borders and enemy movements. Requires [Masonry](pedia:techs/masonry).
workerJobs.barricade: Workers strengthen an existing fortress with heavier defences. A barricade gives defenders even more protection than a plain fortress, making it a strongpoint that is very hard to take. Requires [Construction](pedia:techs/construction).

experienceLevels.conscript: Raw recruits with little training. Conscripts have the fewest hit points and the lowest chance of retreating from a losing fight.
experienceLevels.regular: Trained soldiers, the standard for most units built. Regulars have more hit points than conscripts and a better chance of escaping a losing battle.
experienceLevels.veteran: Battle-hardened troops who have proven themselves. Veterans are tougher and better at retreating, and cities with barracks produce units at this level.
experienceLevels.elite: The best soldiers in the world. Elite units have the most hit points, and an elite unit that wins a battle may produce a great leader.

difficulties.chieftain: The easiest level: your cities have many content citizens, rival civilizations research slowly, and your units get a large bonus against barbarians.
difficulties.warlord: Still forgiving: rivals research more slowly than you, and your cities stay content more easily than at higher levels.
difficulties.regent: The balanced level, where computer players have no special advantages or handicaps.
difficulties.monarch: Computer players begin with extra units and free unit support, research slightly faster than you, and are harder to bargain with.
difficulties.emperor: Computer players get more starting units, more support and faster research, and your cities have fewer content citizens.
difficulties.demigod: Computer players begin with extra settlers and workers and a sizeable army, and grow quickly; only experienced players should try it.
difficulties.deity: Computer players begin with large advantages in units, research and support, and you must play very efficiently to keep up.
difficulties.sid: The hardest level: computer players start with huge armies, extra settlers and workers, and research far faster than you.
